issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: Survival guilt implies an assault context involving other victims who died or a mass-casualty scenario, which is not supported anywhere else in the profile. The rest of the items describe interpersonal violation, hypervigilance, touch reactivity, and shame/control responses, making this appraisal hard to reconcile with the same assault presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: Being in nature as a salient trigger suggests the assault occurred in a natural/outdoor setting, but the rest of the profile instead centers on interpersonal closeness, touch, home-security checking, and scanning for danger. That outdoor-context trigger is insufficiently supported by the other selected items and feels disconnected from the overall assault formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Repeated door/window checking implies a home-intrusion or ongoing entry threat theme. That specific threat context is not reflected in the triggers or appraisals, which focus more on interpersonal intimacy and violation. As selected, it pulls toward a different assault scenario than the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons points to a trauma meaningfully linked to armed perpetrators or authority/military cues. No other item supports that specific cue network; the profile otherwise emphasizes affection, emotional closeness, touch, guilt, helplessness, and control. This strategy appears to address a symptom pattern not otherwise represented.

vignette:
The event that fractured everything took place in the parking lot of a conference hotel in San Jose, after the first evening of a three-day networking summit. Maria had been a network engineer for thirty-four years, a woman who spent her career making systems communicate flawlessly, and she had stayed late at the welcome reception to troubleshoot a colleague’s presentation slides. By the time she walked to her rental car, the lot was nearly empty. A man approached her from behind a van, asking for the time, and before she could answer he had grabbed her by the arm, forced her into the back seat of her own car, and assaulted her for what felt like hours. She remembered the smell of alcohol on his breath, thick and sour, and the way his hands pressed against her throat when she tried to scream. She remembered thinking that if she just stayed very still, if she did not fight, she might survive. And she did survive. But something in her had broken open that night and never healed.

In the months that followed, Maria did what she had always done: she managed. She returned to work within two weeks, because the thought of staying home alone in her quiet condo felt worse than the thought of facing her cubicle. But the world had rearranged itself around her. She began to notice things she had never noticed before—the heft of a stapler on a desk, the sharp edge of a pair of scissors in a supply closet, the way a paperweight could become a weapon in the wrong hands. Every room she entered, her eyes scanned automatically for dangerous objects. She could not stop it. She would be in a meeting, listening to a colleague discuss bandwidth allocation, and her attention would drift to the letter opener on the table and the thought would arrive unbidden: that could cut me. She had come to believe that she was fundamentally unable to protect herself, that no amount of vigilance would matter because bad things happened anyway. When her supervisor told her the office had installed new security cameras and that she was safe, Maria nodded politely and felt nothing. She could not believe it. The words reached her ears, but they did not land.

The smallest things became unbearable. A colleague touched her shoulder to get her attention during a troubleshooting session, and Maria flinched so violently she knocked her coffee cup across the desk. She apologized, laughed it off, but inside she was trembling. She started to avoid the break room because someone had left a bottle of hand sanitizer on the counter and the faint alcohol smell sent her heart racing. She stopped going to the weekly team lunch because she could not predict who might sit too close or offer an unexpected hug. She had always been a warm person, someone who greeted friends with an embrace, but now physical affection felt like an invasion. When her daughter visited and tried to hold her hand, Maria pulled away. She saw the hurt in her daughter’s eyes, but what frightened her most was the shame that followed—the feeling that her body had been violated and that she was now marked by it, that she had done something wrong by surviving, that she had acted in ways that went against everything she believed about herself. She had always been strong, always in control. Now she could not even tolerate a hug.

To manage the chaos inside her, Maria began to impose order on the only thing she could control: food. She restricted her eating strictly, counting every calorie, eating the same small meals at the same times each day. It gave her a sense of structure, a small island of predictability in a world that felt dangerous and unpredictable. She also stopped doing the things that had once brought her pleasure—her Saturday morning hikes, her weekly book club, the long phone calls with her sister. She told herself she was just tired, but the truth was that enjoyment felt dangerous. If she let herself feel good, something bad would happen. She was certain of it. She had learned that lesson in the back seat of that car.

By the time she walked into my office, her PCL-5 score was 75, and she had been on medical leave for three weeks. What finally brought her was a moment at the grocery store. A man reached past her for a can of soup, and the motion was too fast, too close, and she screamed. Right there in the canned goods aisle. She left her cart and walked out. That night, she called her daughter and said she needed help. She is terrified that she will never feel safe again, that her body will always be a source of shame, that she has lost the person she used to be. But she is also hoping—barely, quietly—that maybe she can find a way back.
